title: Astronomers Discover 'Backward' Exoplanet That Orbits Its Star Upside Down
summary: Astronomers have found an exoplanet that orbits its star backward — like a rubber duck spinning against the current in a whirlpool. The planet, called GJ 3090 b, circles a small, red star in the opposite direction of the star's spin. This is called a retrograde orbit, and it's a mystery how it formed. Normally, stars and planets form from the same rotating disk of gas and dust, called a protoplanetary disk. Newly formed objects rotate in the same direction as the disk, because flipping the direction requires a lot of energy applied in just the right way. Astronomers have seen retrograde exoplanets before, but those orbits usually happen when the gravity of other massive objects scrambles the planets' paths. This system, however, doesn't seem to have any massive objects that could have done that. "We looked for the kind of massive companion that could have forced the planet into such an extreme orbit," said study co-author Yann Carteret, an astronomer at the University of Geneva. "We may need to think differently about how this system acquired its unusual architecture." The team analyzed 23 hours of observations from two instruments on a 12-foot-wide (3.6 meters) telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. They watched the planet cross in front of its star 10 times. Each transit dimmed the starlight slightly, revealing the planet's size and orbit. The star is an M dwarf — small, cool and dim. About three-quarters of the stars in the Milky Way are M dwarfs, so studying them is key to understanding our galaxy's exoplanets. The system has two or possibly three planets smaller than Neptune, each orbiting in less than 16 days. GJ 3090 b is the innermost, completing an orbit every 2.9 days. Its orbit is misaligned by 136 degrees — nearly upside down, similar to Venus in our solar system. Because it's closest to the star, it's unlikely a massive planet or hidden binary star disturbed it. The other planets aren't upside down either. Instead, researchers suggest the planet may have been born upside down. If a lot of gas and dust from outside the system got sucked in, it might have replaced the original protoplanetary disk with a second disk at a different angle, forming the retrograde planet. "The idea that a planetary system could be rebuilt from a second, differently oriented disk is particularly exciting," said co-author Vincent Bourrier. "It suggests that the environment around a young star can play a much bigger role in determining the architecture of its planets than we might have expected."
why_it_matters: If a young star's surroundings can rebuild a planetary system from a second, differently angled disk, then how planets end up arranged may depend as much on the environment as on the star itself — which matters for working out how common solar systems like ours are, and whether any of those distant worlds could support life.

background_read: Astronomers confirmed the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star in the 1990s, and since then the count has grown into the thousands. Many were found using the transit method — watching for the small dip in a star's light when a planet crosses in front of it.

Space telescopes like NASA's Kepler (which stared at one patch of sky for years and discovered thousands of planets) and TESS turned planet-hunting into a mass survey, and showed that odd, close-in worlds are common across the galaxy.

Our own solar system is not perfectly tidy either: Venus spins in the opposite direction from most planets, and Uranus is tipped over on its side. Those quirks hint that dramatic events early in a system's life can tilt things permanently.

GJ 3090 b orbits an M dwarf — the small, cool, dim stars that make up about three-quarters of the stars in the Milky Way (the galaxy we live in). Because M dwarfs are faint, close-in planets are relatively easy to detect, making them prime targets in the search for worlds beyond our solar system.

The telescope sits at La Silla Observatory (a telescope site in Chile's Atacama Desert run by the European Southern Observatory), and co-author Yann Carteret is an astronomer at the University of Geneva (a Swiss university with a long history of planet-hunting).

perspectives.description: For them the finding is exciting because it challenges the tidy textbook picture of planet formation and shows that a modest telescope and long observation campaigns can still turn up surprises. It also matters because M dwarfs are the most common stars, so understanding their planets means understanding most planetary systems in the galaxy.

They would note that the evidence rests on a single system and 10 transits, and that the 'second disk' idea is a hypothesis with no direct observation behind it. Other explanations — an undiscovered companion, or the star's own spin axis being measured imperfectly — cannot yet be ruled out.

Retrograde and highly misaligned planets have been seen before, usually blamed on gravitational chaos caused by a massive neighbour. What makes GJ 3090 b different is the apparent absence of such a neighbour, suggesting planetary systems are messier and more varied than our own orderly solar system implies.

The next step is to hunt for any hidden massive companion with more precise instruments, watch more transits, and check whether other star systems show signs of being reshaped by a second disk. Each new example would test whether this is a rare accident or a common way planets are born.
